verses.text: Remember also your Creator in the days of your youth, before the evil days come, and the years draw near, when you will say, “I have no pleasure in them”;
Before the sun, the light, the moon, and the stars are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain;
in the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those who look out of the windows are darkened,
and the doors shall be shut in the street; when the sound of the grinding is low, and one shall rise up at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of music shall be brought low;

yes, they shall be afraid of heights, and terrors will be on the way; and the almond tree shall blossom, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail; because man goes to his everlasting home, and the mourners go about the streets:
before the silver cord is severed, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is broken at the spring, or the wheel broken at the cistern,
and the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
“Vanity of vanities,” says the Preacher. “All is vanity!”
Further, because the Preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge. Yes, he pondered, sought out, and set in order many proverbs.
The Preacher sought to find out acceptable words, and that which was written blamelessly, words of truth.
The words of the wise are like goads; and like nails well fastened are words from the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.
Furthermore, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
This is the end of the matter. All has been heard. Fear God, and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man.
For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.

footnotes.content: The old Preacher speaks from the years beyond, and his words ache with a tender urgency: remember your Maker now, while your days are full of light and strength. Not when the pleasures have dimmed and the body grows heavy—then remembering is harder, though still possible. Grace meets us wherever we turn, but oh, how much sweeter it is when we turn early.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is no cheerless poem about getting old—it's an invitation wrapped in a warning. The light that once seemed endless will grow dim if we spend our vigor chasing what cannot satisfy. The clouds gather all our lives; the Preacher asks us: what will we have tended to when that day comes?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The keepers of the house are our limbs and sinews; the strong men are our bones bowing under time's weight; the grinders that cease are teeth loosening and appetite fading. I know this ancient language of the body well by now—and I've learned it speaks what the soul often ignores. The Lord tends us even as we crumble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The world grows quieter—the sound of the pestle stops, the voice of the bird wakes you too early, the music that once made you dance moves further away. But notice: the Preacher doesn't say we become deaf to the Lord. If anything, when lesser clamor fades, His still, small voice grows clearer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The blossoming almond—white with age, not blooms of youth—marks the paradox of growing old: we can be more beautiful in silver than in gold, if we've been faithful. The grasshopper becomes a burden not because it is heavy, but because we are weaker; yet a weaker vessel poured into by the Lord holds more grace than strength ever could.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The silver cord, the golden bowl, the pitcher, the wheel—each one precious, each one frail. The Preacher speaks in gentle metaphors because the thing itself is hard to bear. But listen beneath: he is saying that our lives are held by God's care, strand by delicate strand, until He gently opens His hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the true victory the Preacher has been moving toward all along. The dust returns—but the spirit? The spirit returns to God who gave it. Death is not an ending but a homecoming; the temporary returns to the eternal. In this verse, vanity breaks like a shell, and what remains is the only thing that ever truly mattered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Preacher speaks his great refrain one more time, and now it doesn't sound like defeat—it sounds like clarity, like a man standing on solid ground. All is vanity, yes. But vanity isn't meaninglessness; it's a plea to look elsewhere, to someone who doesn't vanish. That someone is waiting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Preacher was wise, and precisely because he was, he did not keep wisdom locked away in his own heart. He pondered—turned things over, held them up to the light—and then he taught. This is the work of a true elder: not to pretend certainty, but to share the hard-won search itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He sought not just any words, but acceptable words—words that would hit true, that wouldn't lie to spare feelings or hide truth to avoid offense. And words of truth: he cared more for honesty than for comfort. A teacher like this has walked through suffering himself and come out loving people too much to deceive them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The words of the wise are like goads—they prick us awake when we are drowsy; they are like nails well fastened, holding steady when we would slip. And all these sharp and steadying words come from one Shepherd. Can you hear in this verse the Preacher pointing beyond himself to the one Shepherd of us all?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even the Preacher, wise as he was, warns against endless accumulation—of books, of knowledge, of complexity. The flesh grows weary chasing completion. I've learned this late: that knowing everything is not the same as knowing Him. A single page held close to the heart beats a library held at arm's length.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the whole matter in a sentence: fear God and keep His commandments. Not because you'll get rich or comfortable—the Preacher has already disabused you of that. But because this is the duty, the calling, the deep rightness of a life oriented toward the One who made you. Everything else is commentary.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse that the Preacher lived long before: God will bring every work into judgment, and nothing is hidden from Him. We live after the cross now; judgment for those who trust Jesus has already been borne by Him. Yet the word still stands: live as one whose deeds are known and beloved by the God who sees all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
